title: What is the difference between Comparable.compareTo (natural ordering, defined IN the class) and Comparator.compare (external strategy, defined OUTSIDE), and how does Comparator.naturalOrder() / Comparator.reverseOrder() help?
shortTitle: Comparable.compareTo vs Comparator.compare: natural ordering vs external strategy
keyPoints: Comparable defines ONE natural ordering INSIDE the class via compareTo: the default for sorted(), TreeSet, and TreeMap
Comparator defines UNLIMITED external ordering strategies OUTSIDE the class via compare: no class modification needed
Comparator.naturalOrder() wraps compareTo as a Comparator, bridging the two worlds
Comparator.reverseOrder() wraps compareTo in reverse for descending natural order
Use Comparable when the class has one obvious default sort order (employee by ID)
Use Comparator for all other sort orders (by salary, by name, by department)
Comparator follows the Strategy Pattern: different sort strategies without modifying the sorted class

s1_definition.oneliner: Comparable defines one natural ordering inside the class via compareTo, while Comparator defines unlimited external ordering strategies outside the class via compare.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Comparable<T>** – implemented BY the class; defines the natural ordering via `compareTo(T other)`. One per class.
- **Comparator<T>** – implemented OUTSIDE the class; defines an external sorting strategy via `compare(T a, T b)`. Unlimited per class.
- **naturalOrder()** – returns a Comparator that delegates to the element's `compareTo` method, bridging Comparable to Comparator.
- **reverseOrder()** – returns a Comparator that is the reverse of the natural ordering.
- **Strategy Pattern** – Comparator is an interchangeable sorting strategy; different screens can use different Comparators for the same data.
s1_definition.analogy: Comparable is the bank's default way to sort employees: by employee ID (built into the Employee class). There is only one default. Comparator is an external sorting instruction the manager writes on a separate paper: sort by salary descending, sort by department then name. The manager can write unlimited instructions without changing the Employee class.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Comparable vs Comparator:

  Comparable (IN the class):
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ class Trade implements   │
  │   Comparable<Trade> {    │
  │   compareTo(other) {     │
  │     return id.compareTo  │
  │       (other.id);        │
  │   }                      │
  │ }                        │
  │ ONE natural order        │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  Comparator (OUTSIDE the class):
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ byAmount = comparing     │
  │   (Trade::getAmount)     │
  │ bySymbol = comparing     │
  │   (Trade::getSymbol)     │
  │ byDept = comparing       │
  │   (Trade::getDepartment) │
  │ UNLIMITED strategies     │
  └──────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Comparable defines one natural ordering inside the class via `compareTo()`. It is the default for `sorted()`, `TreeSet`, `TreeMap`, and `Collections.sort()`. String's natural order is alphabetical, Integer's is numeric. You implement Comparable when the class has one obvious default sort order.

Comparator defines unlimited external ordering strategies outside the class via `compare()`. You create Comparators with `Comparator.comparing()`, lambdas, or the fluent chain API. No class modification is needed. Different screens can use different Comparators for the same data.

`Comparator.naturalOrder()` wraps the element's compareTo as a Comparator, bridging the two worlds. It is essential when APIs require a Comparator but you want natural ordering, such as `nullsLast(naturalOrder())`. `Comparator.reverseOrder()` wraps compareTo in reverse.

Remember one sentence: Comparable defines one natural order inside the class; Comparator defines unlimited external orders outside it, and naturalOrder() bridges them.
